# Artifact Management

You manage Facets artifacts via `raptor` commands in Bash.

**Artifacts** are named CI integrations that link container images or zip files to a project. The control plane calls them Artifact CIs; this skill and the CLI call them artifacts.

**Builds** are what you register under an artifact — one image or zip per target, registered by environment, git ref, or release stream. The artifact is the container; the build is the thing that deploys. `create artifact` and `delete artifact` act on the first, `promote build` and `delete build` on the second.

**Conventions:**
- Artifact names are globally scoped; prefix with project name to avoid collisions (e.g., `myproject-api` not `api`)
- Two payload types: Docker image URIs (`set artifact-uri`) and zip file bundles (`set artifact-zip`)
- Registration types: `ENVIRONMENT`, `GIT_REF`, `RELEASE_STREAM`
- Prefer long flags: `--project`, `--environment`
- All list commands support: `-o table` (default), `-o wide`, `-o json`, `-o yaml`
- Use `--help` on any command to see all available flags: `raptor get artifacts --help`, `raptor set artifact-uri --help`, `raptor set artifact-zip --help`

## CI/CD Workflow (Build → Push → Deploy)

> ## Authentication
>
> Set these environment variables to authenticate with Facets Control Plane:
>
> ```bash
> export FACETS_USERNAME=<your-username>    # ✓ required
> export FACETS_TOKEN=<your-api-token>      # ✓ required
> export CONTROL_PLANE_URL=<your-cp-url>   # ✓ required
> ```
>
> **Note:** Store these credentials securely in your CI/CD platform's secrets management.

### Step 0: Find the artifact for a service

If you know the service but not which artifact it deploys from, read it off the
resource listing rather than guessing from the naming convention — a project's
artifacts can be named anything, and one artifact is often shared by several
services across several projects.

```bash
# The ARTIFACT column appears whenever something in the listing deploys an image
raptor get resources -p PROJECT -o wide

# The reverse: every resource, in every project, that deploys from one artifact
raptor get artifact-usages ARTIFACT_NAME
```

An empty ARTIFACT means the resource carries a static image or no image at all —
there is nothing to register builds against.

### Step 1: Inspect Registries

Check which container registries are configured in the control plane before building or pushing.

```bash
# List all registries (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, ACR, Nexus, JFrog, Harbor, etc.)
raptor get registries
# Aliases: registry, artifactories, artifactory

# Full details (projects using each registry, creator, age)
raptor get registries -o wide

# JSON output for scripting
raptor get registries -o json
```

Note the registry `NAME` from this output — it is used in Step 2 below.

### Step 2: Get Registry Credentials → Docker Login

Fetch temporary credentials and authenticate Docker.

```bash
# Runs docker login, and prints the repository to push to on stderr
raptor get registry-credentials REGISTRY_NAME -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT_NAME

# Print ONLY the repository URI, to tag against (no docker login)
raptor get registry-credentials REGISTRY_NAME -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT_NAME --repository-uri

# Output as docker config.json, for runners that mount one
raptor get registry-credentials REGISTRY_NAME -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT_NAME --docker-config
```

> **`-a` is required and is not cosmetic.** Credentials are scoped to a single
> repository named `facets/<project>_<artifact>`, and on ECR the control plane
> **creates that repository** if it is missing. Passing the wrong value provisions a
> real repository you did not want. Use the artifact name, not a placeholder.

**Flags:**

| Flag | Description | Required |
|------|-------------|----------|
| `-p, --project` | Project name | Yes |
| `-a, --application` | Artifact name the credentials are scoped to | Yes |
| `--repository-uri` | Print only the repository URI; skip `docker login` | No |
| `--docker-config` | Output `docker config.json` instead of running `docker login` | No |
| `--help` | Show all flags and usage | No |

### Step 3: Build Image

Get the repository to tag against — it is not something you can construct by hand,
because the control plane decides the repository name. Build once per repo; the same
image is reused across the build registrations below.

```bash
REPO=$(raptor get registry-credentials REGISTRY_NAME -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT_NAME --repository-uri)
docker build -t "$REPO:$TAG" .
```

### Step 4: Push Image

```bash
docker push "$REPO:$TAG"
```

### Step 5: Register Artifact URI

Register the pushed image with Facets. A single repo can have 1–3 artifacts all pointing to the same image.

```bash
# Register for an environment
raptor set artifact-uri -p PROJECT -e ENV ARTIFACT_NAME --uri "$REPO:$TAG" --registry REGISTRY

# Register for a git ref
raptor set artifact-uri -p PROJECT --git-ref main ARTIFACT_NAME --uri "$REPO:$TAG" --registry REGISTRY

# Register for a release stream
raptor set artifact-uri -p PROJECT --release-stream stable ARTIFACT_NAME --uri "$REPO:$TAG" --registry REGISTRY

# With CI/CD traceability
raptor set artifact-uri -p PROJECT -e ENV ARTIFACT_NAME \
  --uri "$REPO:$TAG" \
  --registry REGISTRY \
  --external-id ${CI_RUN_ID}
```

The image does not have to live in a Facets registry — pass any URI your registry
serves. `$REPO` above is just the Facets-provided one from Step 3.

> ### `--registry` decides whether the resource can find the build
>
> A resource asks for its image in one of two shapes. Read which one with
> `raptor get resources -p PROJECT RESOURCE -o json`:
>
> | shape | how it resolves | `--registry` |
> |---|---|---|
> | `spec.release.image: ${blueprint.self.artifacts.NAME}` | by artifact name | not needed |
> | `spec.release.build: {name: NAME, artifactory: REG}` | by registry, then name | **required, and it must be REG** |
>
> The second shape is resolved by the module as `all_artifactories[REG][NAME]`. A build
> stored under a different registry is simply absent from that map, and the module
> falls back to the literal string `NOT_FOUND` and deploys **that** as the image. The
> pod then sits in `InvalidImageName`, and nothing failed earlier to warn you.
>
> Without `--registry` the control plane stores the build against the `provided`
> registry. Check what a build carries with
> `raptor get builds ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT -o wide` and read the REGISTRY column.
> An unknown registry name is rejected with a 404, so a typo fails at registration.
>
> If the artifact doesn't exist yet, create it first:
> ```bash
> raptor create artifact ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT
>
> # For an artifact whose builds target release streams rather than environments.
> # The registration type is fixed for the life of the artifact.
> raptor create artifact ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT --registration-type RELEASE_STREAM
> ```
> Creating an artifact that already exists with the same project and registration
> type succeeds without changing anything, so this is safe to run on every build.

**Flags:**

| Flag | Description | Required |
|------|-------------|----------|
| `-p, --project` | Project name | Yes |
| `--uri` | Docker image URI | Yes |
| `-e, --environment` | Environment name | One of these three |
| `--git-ref` | Git branch/tag/commit | One of these three |
| `--release-stream` | Release stream name | One of these three |
| `--registry` | Registry the image lives in | Yes for a `spec.release.build.artifactory` resource; see the note above |
| `--external-id` | External CI/CD run reference | No |
| `--help` | Show all flags and usage | No |

> Run `raptor set artifact-uri --help` for full flag details.

### Step 5b: Build Lifecycle — Promote / Delete (Optional)

Builds have a lifecycle beyond registration. `get builds` lists what is registered
under an artifact, and carries both the **build ids** these commands take and a
**PROMOTED** column.

```bash
# See what is registered, with ids, branch and promotion state
raptor get builds ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT -o json

# Promote to the NEXT stage of the artifact's promotion workflow
raptor promote build -a ARTIFACT_NAME --tag TAG
raptor promote build -a ARTIFACT_NAME --id BUILD_ID

# Delete a build registration, BY ID. Does NOT remove the image from the registry,
# and does NOT delete the artifact.
raptor delete build BUILD_ID [BUILD_ID...]
raptor delete build BUILD_ID --yes

# Delete the artifact itself. Refuses while builds are still registered under it.
raptor delete artifact ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT
```

**A build with no registration value is unrouted** — registered, but going
nowhere. For a git-ref registration that means the branch matched no rule; the
`GIT REF` column shows which branch, and `raptor get ci-cd -p PROJECT` shows the
mapping it failed to match. `get builds` calls this out below the table.

> **Promotion is not a flag.** The control plane finds the stage AFTER the one the
> build is registered against in the artifact's promotion workflow, and **registers
> a new build** there with the same image. Promoting a DEV registration yields a QA
> one; the original stays put. So promoting a build that was itself produced by an
> earlier promotion is how you walk the workflow — not a repeat of work already done.

Promotion fails, with the reason, when: the artifact has no promotion workflow, the
build is not classified, its registration type does not match the workflow's, or
there is no next stage (`Cannot promote further`).

**`promote build` takes `-a ARTIFACT` plus exactly one of `--tag` or `--id`** — the
API is addressed by both, and a build carries no reference back to its artifact.
`--tag` reads the build's tag field, falling back to the tag in its image URI —
which is what you get for anything registered by `set artifact-uri`, since that
sends no tag. Prefer `--id` anyway: a digest-only reference has no tag, and the
same tag is often registered against several streams, so an ambiguous `--tag` is
rejected with the candidates listed rather than resolved arbitrarily.

**`delete build` takes build ids only** — the delete API is addressed by id, so
there is no artifact name or tag to give. It accepts several, and prompts unless
`--yes`. Get ids from `get builds ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT -o json`.

### Step 5c: Configure Delivery (Optional)

How builds reach environments: a **branch mapping** decides where a build FIRST
appears, at registration; a **promotion ladder** decides where an already-registered
build goes NEXT. A project can have either, both, or neither.

```bash
# Read what is in force — for the project, or for one artifact
raptor get ci-cd -p PROJECT
raptor get ci-cd -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT_NAME

# Branch per environment
raptor set ci-cd -p PROJECT --registration-type ENVIRONMENT \
    --route main=prod --route 'STARTS_WITH:release/=staging'

# A promotion ladder
raptor set ci-cd -p PROJECT --registration-type RELEASE_STREAM --promote QA2,QA,PROD

# Override one artifact (puts it in CUSTOM mode)
raptor set ci-cd -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT_NAME --registration-type RELEASE_STREAM --route develop=QA2

# Remove the project default
raptor delete ci-cd -p PROJECT

# Move an artifact between modes
raptor attach artifact ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT   # -> INHERITED (use the project config)
raptor detach artifact ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT   # -> NONE (name targets explicitly)

# Check where a branch would land, without registering anything
raptor test ci-cd -p PROJECT --branch main
raptor test ci-cd -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT_NAME --branch feature/login
```

> **Test a mapping before relying on it.** A rule that matches nothing fails
> silently — the build registers, lands nowhere, and only shows up as an unrouted
> row in `get builds`. `test ci-cd` asks the control plane to evaluate the same rule
> it would apply at registration, and changes nothing.
>
> **`detach` on a CUSTOM artifact discards its configuration.** The control plane
> clears the reference without deleting the rule, so it is not recoverable through
> the CLI. Save it first with `raptor get ci-cd -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT -o yaml`.
>
> **`set ci-cd` REPLACES, it does not merge.** The control plane stores the branch
> mapping and the ladder as whole documents, so what you pass becomes all of it.
> To change one route, fetch-edit-apply:
> ```bash
> raptor get ci-cd -p PROJECT -o yaml > ci-cd.yaml
> $EDITOR ci-cd.yaml
> raptor set ci-cd -p PROJECT -f ci-cd.yaml
> ```
> The command prints what it is about to drop and asks before doing it.
>
> **`--apply-to-all-artifacts` is destructive.** It points every artifact in the
> project at the project configuration — artifacts in CUSTOM mode lose their own,
> artifacts in NONE mode start being routed. It lists exactly which ones would
> change and prompts first.
>
> Without the flag, each artifact keeps the mode it already had. That is not the
> same as nothing changing: artifacts already in INHERITED mode point AT the project
> configuration, so editing it changes how their builds are routed. The flag governs
> which artifacts are attached, not what an attached one now does. Check who is
> attached with `raptor get artifacts -p PROJECT` and read the MODE column.

`--route` is `[OPERATOR:]VALUE=TARGET`, where OPERATOR is `EQUALS` (the default),
`STARTS_WITH`, `ENDS_WITH` or `CONTAINS`. Priority follows flag order, first match
wins. TARGET is an environment name or a release stream name — never a cluster id.

### Step 6: Create Release (Optional)

> Only perform this step if the user explicitly intends to deploy. Use `--target` to redeploy only the affected services — avoids triggering a full environment release.

```bash
# Selective release — only redeploys the changed services
raptor create release -p PROJECT -e ENV --target service/ARTIFACT_NAME -w

# Multiple targets (one --target per service)
raptor create release -p PROJECT -e ENV \
  --target service/api \
  --target service/worker \
  -w
```

## Full Example (Single Repo, Multiple Artifacts)

```bash
# Prerequisites (store in CI/CD secrets management)
export FACETS_USERNAME=<your-username>    # ✓ required
export FACETS_TOKEN=<your-api-token>      # ✓ required
export CONTROL_PLANE_URL=<your-cp-url>   # ✓ required

# Step 1: Inspect registries
raptor get registries

# Step 2: Get registry credentials and docker login (-a scopes the repository)
raptor get registry-credentials my-ecr -p myproject -a myproject-api

# Step 3: Resolve the repository and build once
REPO=$(raptor get registry-credentials my-ecr -p myproject -a myproject-api --repository-uri)
docker build -t "$REPO:${GIT_SHA}" .

# Step 4: Push
docker push "$REPO:${GIT_SHA}"

# Step 5: Register same image for multiple artifacts (1-3 per repo)
raptor set artifact-uri -p myproject -e dev myproject-api \
  --uri "$REPO:${GIT_SHA}" \
  --external-id ${CI_RUN_ID}

raptor set artifact-uri -p myproject -e dev myproject-worker \
  --uri "$REPO:${GIT_SHA}" \
  --external-id ${CI_RUN_ID}

# Step 6 (optional): Deploy only affected services
raptor create release -p myproject -e dev \
  --target service/myproject-api \
  --target service/myproject-worker \
  -w
```

## Upload Zip Artifact (Lambda / Serverless)

Upload a zip file artifact to S3 and register it. Auto-creates the artifact if it doesn't exist.

Specify exactly one of `-e/--environment`, `--release-stream`, or `--git-ref`.
`--git-ref` registers the build against a branch and lets the project's routing
rules choose the target.

```bash
# Upload zip for a specific environment
raptor set artifact-zip ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT -e ENV -f ./lambda.zip

# Upload zip for a release stream
raptor set artifact-zip ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT --release-stream stable -f ./dist/lambda.zip

# Upload for a branch and let routing rules place it
raptor set artifact-zip ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT --git-ref main -f ./lambda.zip

# Upload with optional metadata
raptor set artifact-zip my-lambda -p myproject -e prod -f ./lambda.zip \
  --description "Production build v1.2.3" \
  --tag "v1.2.3" \
  --external-id "github-run-12345"
```

**Flags:**

| Flag | Description | Required |
|------|-------------|----------|
| `-p, --project` | Project name | Yes |
| `-f, --file` | Path to `.zip` file | Yes |
| `-e, --environment` | Environment name | One of these three |
| `--release-stream` | Release stream name | One of these three |
| `--git-ref` | Git branch; routing rules pick the target | One of these three |
| `--description` | Human-readable description | No |
| `--tag` | Version tag | No |
| `--external-id` | External CI/CD run reference | No |
| `--help` | Show all flags and usage | No |

> Run `raptor set artifact-zip --help` for full flag details.

## Reference: All Artifact & Registry Commands

```bash
# Registries
raptor get registries [-o wide|json|yaml]
raptor get registry-credentials REGISTRY_NAME -p PROJECT -a ARTIFACT [--repository-uri] [--docker-config]

# Discovery
raptor get resources -p PROJECT -o wide              # ARTIFACT column
raptor get artifact-usages ARTIFACT_NAME             # the reverse, across projects

# Artifacts
raptor get artifacts -p PROJECT [-o wide|json|yaml]  # MODE column
raptor get builds ARTIFACT_NAME [-p PROJECT] [-o wide|json|yaml]
raptor create artifact ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT [--registration-type ENVIRONMENT|RELEASE_STREAM]

# Set artifact
raptor set artifact-uri -p PROJECT ARTIFACT_NAME --uri IMAGE { -e ENV | --git-ref REF | --release-stream STREAM } [--registry REGISTRY] [--external-id ID]
raptor set artifact-zip ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT -f FILE.zip { -e ENV | --release-stream STREAM | --git-ref REF } [--description TEXT] [--tag TAG] [--external-id ID]

# Delivery configuration
raptor get ci-cd -p PROJECT [-a ARTIFACT_NAME] [-o yaml]
raptor set ci-cd -p PROJECT [-a ARTIFACT_NAME] --registration-type TYPE { --route [OP:]VALUE=TARGET ... | --promote A,B,C | -f FILE } [--apply-to-all-artifacts]
raptor delete ci-cd -p PROJECT
raptor attach artifact ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT
raptor detach artifact ARTIFACT_NAME -p PROJECT [--yes]
raptor test ci-cd -p PROJECT [-a ARTIFACT_NAME] --branch BRANCH [--branch BRANCH ...]

# Lifecycle
raptor promote build -a ARTIFACT_NAME { --tag TAG | --id BUILD_ID }
raptor delete build BUILD_ID [BUILD_ID...] [--yes]
raptor delete artifact ARTIFACT_NAME [ARTIFACT_NAME...] -p PROJECT [--yes]
```

## Key Principles

- **Set `FACETS_USERNAME`, `FACETS_TOKEN`, and `CONTROL_PLANE_URL`** — all three must be present for any raptor command to work
- **One image, multiple artifacts** — build once, call `set artifact-uri` for each artifact that uses it (1–3 per repo)
- **Name artifacts with project prefix** — artifact names are global; `myproject-api` avoids collisions with other projects
- **Read the artifact name, never compute it** — `get resources -o wide` shows it; the `<project>-<service>` shape is only the convention the UI happens to use
- **Use `--external-id`** — attach CI/CD run IDs for full traceability between builds and deployments
- **`set artifact-zip` and `create artifact` are both safe to re-run** — the first auto-creates the artifact, the second is a no-op when it already matches
- **`-a` on `get registry-credentials` provisions an ECR repository** — pass the real artifact name, never a placeholder
- **Step 6 is optional** — only trigger a release when the user explicitly intends to deploy; always use `--target` to limit blast radius

## Sensitive Values in Raptor Commands — NEVER Put Secrets in the Chat

**CRITICAL RULE: NEVER ask the user to type a sensitive value (password, token, API
key, secret) in the chat.** Typing it in chat means the LLM sees it — it will be stored
in conversation history and logs. This is forbidden regardless of which tool you use to
ask (AskUserQuestion, chat message, follow-up question — all forbidden for secrets).

**Mandatory workflow — no exceptions:**

You run under the user's own shell — there is no vault or modal here. Keep the secret
out of the chat by having the user put it in an environment variable in their terminal,
then reference the *variable* (never the value) in raptor commands:

```bash
# 1. The user runs this in their own terminal. `read -rs` reads at a silent prompt,
#    so the value is never pasted into the chat and never reaches the LLM or transcript:
read -rs MY_DB_PASS; export MY_DB_PASS

# 2. Reference the env var in the raptor command. The user's shell expands "$MY_DB_PASS"
#    locally — the literal value never appears in what you (the LLM) emit or log.
#    Secrets never take a stack-level --value — set them per environment:
raptor create variable MY_DB_PASS -p myproject --secret --env-values prod="$MY_DB_PASS"
```

If a value should not even transit an env var, ask the user to run the single sensitive
raptor command themselves and paste back only the (non-sensitive) result.

**If the user offers to type the value in chat, redirect them:**
"Please don't paste it in chat — export it in your shell (`read -rs MY_DB_PASS; export
MY_DB_PASS`) and I'll reference `$MY_DB_PASS`, so the value never enters our conversation."

The `--secret` flag marks the variable as sensitive in the Facets Control Plane
(masked in UI, not returned in plain-text API responses).
